paper.title: Predicting thermodynamic stability of inorganic compounds using ensemble machine learning based on electron configuration
paper.research_summary: This paper proposes an ensemble machine learning framework—Electron Configuration models with Stacked Generalization (ECSG)—to predict the thermodynamic stability of inorganic compounds. ECSG integrates three base-level models grounded in distinct domain knowledge: Magpie (atomic properties), Roost (interatomic interactions), and ECCNN (electron configuration). The framework uses stacked generalization to combine their outputs into a meta-level model, achieving high predictive accuracy (AUC = 0.988 on JARVIS) and exceptional sample efficiency (requiring only 1/7 the data of existing models). It is validated across multiple databases (MP, OQMD, JARVIS), applied to unknown composition spaces (perovskite halides, Li-containing oxides, transition metal oxides), and deployed in two case studies: discovery of 2D wide bandgap semiconductors and double perovskite oxides—both confirmed via first-principles DFT calculations.

tasks.task_name_raw: Predicting thermodynamic stability of inorganic compounds
tasks.objective: Accurately predict whether an inorganic compound is thermodynamically stable or unstable
constraints: stability defined by decomposition energy ΔHd < 0 meV/atom

evidence.text: Machine learning offers a promising avenue for expediting the discovery of new compounds by accurately predicting their thermodynamic stability.

The thermodynamic stability of materials is typically represented by the decomposition energy (ΔHd)6, which is defined as the total energy difference between a given compound and competing compounds in a specific chemical space.
Compounds with a ΔHd below 0 meV/atom were considered stable and are labeled accordingly.

evidence.text: The input of ECCNN is a matrix with shape of 118 × 168 × 8, which is encoded by the EC of materials.

The construction of the features for ECCNN is illustrated in Fig. 8. The first step involves identifying the categories of elements in the compound. As shown in Fig. 8a, elements oxygen and aluminum are identified from the compound Al2O3. To represent the number of electrons in each subshell, one-hot encoding is employed, as displayed in Fig. 8b.

we slightly relax the threshold restriction when classifying materials stability. Consequently, we utilize thresholds of 25 meV/atom and 40 meV/atom to assign stability labels in the data set.

stages.stage_name_raw: Training base-level models (Magpie, Roost, ECCNN) and meta-level model (MLR)
stages.stage_goal: Train individual base models and then train a meta-level model to combine their predictions

evidence.text: We utilized a highly effective ensemble technique called SG to combine the predictions from these individual models for forecasting the thermodynamic stability of materials.
The base-level models include ECCNN, Roost, and Magpie, denoted as f 1, f 2, and f 3. The meta-level model is a multi-response linear regression (MLR), denoted as F.

stage_input: test sets from MP, OQMD, JARVIS

evidence.text: All models were trained using data sourced from the MP dataset, as detailed in the Methods section. We include several metrics, Area Under the receiver operating characteristic Curve (AUC), accuracy (ACC), Precision, Recall, F1-score (F1), negative predictive values (NPV), and Area Under the Precision-Recall curve (AUPR), to provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

stages.stage_name_raw: Enumerating candidate compounds in unexplored composition space
stages.stage_goal: Systematically generate candidate materials for stability prediction
stage_input: element lists (e.g., metals up to Bi)

evidence.text: We constructed the candidate space of perovskites by enumerating all possible ABO3, A2BB′O6, AA′B2O6, and AA′BB′O6 compounds. In this process, we considered all metal elements up to Bi, resulting in a total of 67 different types of cations that could occupy A-sites or B-sites. This lead to P(67, 2) = 4422 possible ABO3 type perovskites. For A2BB′O6, AA′B2O6, and AA′BB′O6 type perovskites, there were 143,715, 143,715, and 4,598,880 potential combinations, respectively. After filtering for charge neutrality, 4,524,608 unique compounds remained, forming the candidate composition space.

stages.stage_name_raw: Applying ECSG to rank and filter candidate compounds by predicted stability probability
stages.stage_goal: Prioritize candidates most likely to be thermodynamically stable

evidence.text: By setting the cutoff probability to 0.5, we identified 1,877,443 perovskite oxides predicted to be stable, substantially narrowing down our search range.

stages.stage_name_raw: Validating predictions via first-principles DFT calculations
stages.stage_goal: Confirm stability predictions using ab initio energy computations
stage_output: DFT-calculated decomposition energies and convex hull stability assessments

evidence.text: We randomly selected 35 compounds with stability probabilities greater than 90% (63 in total) for first-principles calculations to validate the accuracy of our machine-learning method.

The total energy calculations in this study were performed using the DFT framework as implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)... To construct the convex hull for each set of elements comprising A-A′-B-B′-O, the total energy data of all compounds in the MP database was considered and extracted using the database API.

evidence.text: In this work, we compared the performance of various models in predicting the stability of inorganic compounds on three large DFT-computed datasets, MP, OQMD, and JARVIS.
The same data processing method was applied to the OQMD and JARVIS databases, and datasets in unknown spaces.
First, we extracted the composition and stability information of the materials from the entire C2DB database and trained a model to predict the thermodynamic stability of 2D materials.
Then, we tested the trained model on the 2Dmatpedia database, which contains 4743 materials.
Initially, we compiled a database of 1333 double perovskite oxides. This database served as the basis for training a super learner through ECSG to predict the stability of perovskite oxides.

We collected thermodynamic stability data for 496 perovskite halides from the literature. Among these materials, there are 408 materials in the MP database. To ensure the perovskite halide dataset is independent of the training set, we remove these duplicate samples from MP.
Different from testing in perovskite halides, we extract all materials containing Li and O from MP, resulting in 6168 samples, with 750 stable materials.

In this study, we use Fe-containing oxides and Mn-containing oxides as examples to test the model’s ability to predict unknown transition metal oxides. Similar to our approach with Li-containing oxides, we extracted 7137 transition metal oxides from the MP database and used the remaining data of MP to train the models.
